## Abstract

Background The recent global rise in AIV outbreaks underscores the risk of transmission to humans. This study conducted surveillance to assess AIV circulation in poultry-related environments and patients with PUE in China.

Methods From December 2021 to December 2023, we conducted AIV surveillance in LPMs, slaughterhouses, and poultry farms/backyards, alongside hospitalized PUE patients in East (City A, Nanping city), Central (City B, Luoyang city) and Southwest (City C, Chongqing) China. rRT-PCR was used to detect influenza A, with subtyping for H5, H7, H9, and H10. The median monthly positivity rate of AIVs was calculated, and differences in detection frequency were analyzed using Chi-square tests.

Results Of 8,335 environmental specimens, the median monthly positivity rate for influenza A was 32.6%, with H5 at 6.9% and H9 at 18.4%. H5 was more frequently detected in Chongqing (13.5%), while H9 was highest in Nanping city (25.4%). LPMs and slaughterhouses showed higher positivity rates than farms/backyards, with blood wastewater and cutting board swabs more frequently contaminated than fecal samples and drinking water. Six H10 samples were detected, but no H7. Among 840 PUE respiratory specimens, 86 tested positive for seasonal influenza A, but no human AIV infections were identified.

Conclusion Despite global AIV spread, no significant changes in AIV circulation were observed, and no human infections were detected. H9 remained the dominant subtype, highlighting the need to enhance poultry vaccination. Strengthening bio-security in LPMs and protecting occupationally exposed workers is recommended.

## Background

From December 10, 2020 to January 20, 2025, a total of 348 cases of human infection with AIVs have

been reported globally, including 172 cases of human infection detected in China [1]. Epidemiological

investigations of human infection with AIVs showed that most cases had a history of exposure to

infected poultry or contaminated poultry-related environments before the onset of the disease [2, 3]. From January 2005 to November 2022, there were three waves caused by H5 viruses around the world. In the first wave, the outbreaks were mainly reported in Asian countries while the third wave included outbreaks mainly reported in Europe and North America countries since 2020. A large number of birds were died or destroyed in the third wave, and more than 389 million poultry around the world had been lost being infection with H5 highly pathogenic AIVs. Many countries in Europe and North America control highly pathogenic AIVs by culling alone, whereas some countries, including China, have adopted a strategy of

“cull plus vaccination” [4]. China initiated the H5 poultry vaccination program in 2005 and trivalent H5/H7 poultry vaccination program in 2017, and significantly decreased the outbreaks and the isolation rate of

H5 and H7 AIVs in poultry [5]. Moreover, H9 subtype AIVs sustain high levels circulation in poultry and

wild birds, and play an important role in the evolution of novel AIVs by providing various internal genes

Page 4/21

via gene reassortment. H9 is one of the most likely AIVs subtype to cause a pandemic proposed by WHO

[6, 7].

A global increase of AIVs circulation in poultry and cross species transmission underscores the

increased risk of AIVs transmission to human [8, 9]. There are concerns about probably underestimate

because of insufficient diagnosis and surveillance at the human-animal interface.

This study aims to understand the temporal trends and different geographic distribution characteristics of AIVs in China, and we conducted an enhanced surveillance in poultry-related environments and hospitalized patients with PUE in eastern, central and Southwest China from December 2021 through December 2023.

## Methods

## Study location

Three cities located in East China (City A, Nanping city), Central China (City B, Luoyang city) and Southwest China (City C, Chongqing) were selected as surveillance sites for surveillance by following the criteria of high poultry population for breeding industry and poultry trade, and willingness for collaboration.

## Poultry related environment surveillance

Poultry related environmental surveillance sites included live poultry markets (LPMs), poultry farms/backyards and slaughterhouses. LPMs were defined as fixed wholesale and retailed markets that sell live poultry such as chickens, ducks, geese and quail. Poultry farm or backyard were defined were registered commercially and household farms for commercial operations or personal consumption during the study period. Backyards poultry were selected when the number of poultry farm was limited in the surveillance site. The slaughterhouses were defined as registered fixed workplace to kill live poultry. The types of environmental specimens were poultry drinking water and swabs from fecal droppings, blood sewage on the floor, and the chopping board.

Each collection tube for one type of specimen included pooled specimens of up to three swabs from different locations ( swabs from the different surfaces of one chop board to increase representative). Oral informed consent was obtained from stall operators, poultry farm and slaughterhouse owners before sample collection. Environmental sample collection requirements were shown in Fig. 1.

## Surveillance among inpatients with PUE

The study team selected four general hospitals as surveillance sites in three cities. Three of four were the national influenza sentinel surveillance hospitals. Trained surveillance doctors and nurses enrolled


<!-- Page 5 -->


Page 5/21

PUE inpatients from the department of pulmonary diseases, infectious diseases and respiratory medicine by following the case definition in this study: ① axillary temperature > 38◦C,② radiographic pneumonia; ③No antiviral therapy was given. Oral informed consents were obtained prior to the collection of all respiratory specimens. The study team collected 10 PUE inpatients from surveillance departments of in each surveillance City each month. Either the upper respiratory tract specimen (throat swab, nose swab) or lower respiratory tract specimen (deep sputum, alveolar cleaning fluid) was acceptable, while lower respiratory tract specimens were preferred. Sample collection requirements were shown in Fig. 1.

## Laboratory testing

Both environmental and human specimens were transported and stored according to the national surveillance protocol. Specimens were placed in viral transport media and transported on the same day to local CDC influenza laboratories on frozen gel packs. The specimens were tested for influenza A virus by rRT-PCR within 24h after they received the samples or stored the samples at -70℃ for later test. Influenza A positive specimens were further tested for subtypes H5, H7, H9 and H10 subtype by using specific primers and probes. If specimens were positive for influenza A while negative for subtypes H5, H7, H9 and H10, the test result was defined as "Others". If the specimens were tested positive for more than one subtypes, which was defined as “co-occurrence of subtypes” and the positive samples will be counted separately within their corresponding subtypes. All hospital patients’ respiratory tract specimen were transported to CNIC under dry ice conditions and tested using rRT-PCR. RNA was extracted using RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), and rRT-PCR was conducted as described in the national protocol. And the method for sequencing the genes of H10 subtype positive specimens is the same as

previously described [10].

## Results

## Environmental sample collection

A total of 14 LPMs (six in City A, three in City B, five in City C), 18 poultry farms/backyards (10 in City A, three in City B and five in City C), and 5 poultry slaughterhouses (two in City A, one in City B and two in City C) were selected for surveillance. From December 2021 to December 2023, a total of 8,335 environmental samples were collected in 3 cities, including 2,925 from City A, 2,700 from City B and 2,710 from City C. There were 6,480 environmental samples were collected from LPMs, 1,120 were collected from farms/backyards and 735 were collected from slaughterhouses.

Positivity rate distribution of rRT-PCR testing of avian related environmental samples in three different cities in two surveillance years

The overall monthly median positivity rate for influenza A was 32.6% (15.6%-44.7%) in three surveillance cities. Among them, monthly median positivity rate of H5, H9 and H10 was 6.9%, 18.4% and < 0.1% respectively. None H7 subtype were detected during two surveillance years.

For subtype H5, the highest positivity rate was detected in City C (13.5%), followed by City A (3.7%). The study tested thirteen H10 positive samples in City A, none in City B and City C (Table 1). ## Positivity rates of influenza A subtype among the different sampling sites


<!-- Page 7 -->


Page 7/21

The overall positive rates of influenza A were similar in LPMs and poultry slaughterhouses (35.2% and 35.0%), both were higher than that in farms or backyards (13.3%). For H5, the positivity rates in LPMs

(8.2%) were higher than slaughterhouse (4.9%) and farms/backyard (2.5%), (χ2 = 52, P < 0.05). The H9 subtype positivity rate in slaughterhouses (22.4%) was slightly higher than that in LPMs (21.9%), but both

rates were significantly higher than that in farms/backyard(7.9%), (χ2 = 119, P < 0.05).

The H5 and H9 positive rate by surveillance sites were shown in Fig. 4 and monthly positive rates of H5 (Fig. 5a) and H9 (Fig. 5b) were presented in Fig. 5. H5 and H9 positive rates were generally higher in LPM than poultry farm throughout two surveillance years with few month exceptions. Compared with H5, H9 was more frequently detected with a higher or similar positive rate in poultry farms than LPMs.

## Positivity rates of H5, H9 subtype by category of environmental samples

The monthly median positivity rates of AIVs detections ranked from highest to lowest were chopping boards (8.3% for H5, 21.8% for H9), blood sewage(7.4% for H5,21.5% for H9), feces droppings(4.2%for H5, 16.0% for H9) and poultry drinking water(2.3 for H5%,14.0% for H9) in three surveillance cities from Dec 2021 to Dec 2023, respectively(P < 0.05). Among the four category of samples, the H9 subtype exhibited a higher prevalence. In terms of both H5 and H9 subtypes, the monthly median detection positivity rates of AIVs in chopping board swabs and blood sewage were higher than those in feces dropping and poultry drinking water.

In City A, the median positivity rates of H9 was at relatively high level in four different category of samples, while in City B and City C, the median positivity rates of H9 were generally lower in feces droppings and poultry drinking water than that in chopping boards and blood sewage (Table 3).

Homology analysis of HA1 gene between H10 subtype in this study and isolates from human cases

While H10 subtype AIVs maintain extremely low prevalence in environmental surveillance, 5 sporadic human H10 subtype AIV infections over the past years had been reported. To elucidate this epidemiological paradox, we performed whole-genome sequencing on H10 AIV isolates and conducted homology analysis. There were thirteen H10 subtype AIVs detected in this study were subjected to genetic sequencing (GISAID accession numbers were: EPI4190473-EPI4190482, EPI3497274, EPI3497282, EPI3497290). Sequences analysis revealed two distinct clades within the H10 subtype. Among them, six H10N3 viruses detected in February and March 2022 demonstrated high HA1 gene


<!-- Page 9 -->


Page 9/21

homology (98.9%-99.0%) with the HA1 gene of the human infection with H10N3 avian influenza virus (A/Jiangsu/428/2021(H10N3) ). These six isolates were exclusively collected from fixed stalls in LPMs, with four originating from poultry blood-contaminated wastewater and two from chopping board swabs. Other seven H10 subtype viruses, four were identified as H10N4 and three as H10N3. Sequence alignment via the GISAID database showed the highest homology (96.3%-96.7%) between these seven isolates and an H10N3 virus strain isolated from ducks in Zhejiang Province in 2017, while with human isolates in China were between 91.5% and 94.7%, except A/Zhejiang/CNIC-ZJU01/2023(H10N5). All these thirteen H10 subtype virus showed low HA1 gene homology (80.0%-81.8%) with this H10N5 virus. Detailed specimen information is summarized in Supplementary Material 1 and Supplementary Material 2.

## Influenza and AIVs surveillance in hospitalized PUE patients

A total of 840 respiratory specimens were collected from 840 hospitalized PUE patients of three surveillance cities during the study period. Multiple respiratory specimen types were collected including nasopharyngeal swabs, alveolar lavage fluid, deep sputum, respiratory extracts and sputamentum specimensC. Among those, 86 specimen were tested positive for seasonal influenza viruses, including 83 influenza A, 3 influenza B. None was positive for AIVs. Influenza positives by month and by City was presented in Fig. 6(a-b).

## Discussions

While a widespread of avian influenza virus among poultry globally, our environmental surveillance data from LPMs, farms/backyards, and slaughterhouses showed no significant changes in the spatiotemporal distribution of H5, H7, and H10 compared to that in the previous year, and no human cases infection with AIVs was detected in the surveillance cities. H9 remained the dominant circulating strain, and presented a slight increase compared with the previous year. H5 and H9 positive rates were generally higher in LPM than that in poultry farm, and significantly higher in blood sewage and chopping board swabs.

Poultry farms, particularly breeding farms conducted multiple and regular immunizations for poultry and hatching eggs, which lead to a relatively high antibody positivity rate in poultry.These vaccination

practices played a crucial role in maintaining low level of H7 subtype and H5 subtype [4, 11]. Compared to

LPMs, poultry farms generally implemented strict biosecurity measures, including isolation, disinfection,

closed management, and restrictions on personnel and vehicle access [12]. Furthermore, the relatively uniform, clearer background information of poultry, strict bio-security requirement in poultry farms also

helped mitigate the introduction and spread of the AIV [13]. In large-scale farms, avian influenza outbreaks were more easily identified, leading to the rapid culling of infected poultry to prevent the spread of AIVs. For these reasons, the positive rate of avian influenza virus in poultry farms was

generally lower than that observed in LPMs and slaughterhouses [14].


<!-- Page 10 -->


Page 10/21

City B was located in the northern region, while Cities A and C were situated in the southern region. Typically, the positive rates of avian influenza viruses in northern regions were lower than those in southern regions. Additionally, the sample collection period for this study was during the COVID-19 pandemic, when different regions had different strategies for LPMs, including periodic market closure. Different cities have different sources of poultry. These factors contributed to the disparities in positive rates observed across the cities.

Avian influenza virus surveillance for H5 subtype

Since 2020, HPAIV H5 subtype has caused outbreaks in wild and domestic birds around the world [15–17]. These outbreaks led to the culling of millions of poultry, severely impacting poultry production and

export [18]. Sporadic human infection with HPAIV H5 viruses have been reported during the study period,

notably in China and Vietnam in 2021, and reduced in China since 2022. China has introduced a mass mandatory poultry vaccination program since 2005, and H5 detection in poultry had significantly declined.

Between December 2021 and December 2023, the median monthly nucleic acid positivity rate of H5 subtype in three surveillance cities was 6.9%, ranging from 1.4–15.4%. These findings align with national

surveillance data from 2014–2018 in Southwestern China, which reported rates of 11.4%-13.8% [19]. Despite a global surge in H5 outbreaks and cross-species transmission, our enhanced surveillance showed no significant increase in H5 distribution across China in past two years. Additionally, H5 positivity rates were higher in LPMs and slaughterhouses compared to poultry farms, The result was consistent with previous studies both domestically and internationally. And with higher rates found in blood sewage (9.3%) and chopping board swabs (8.7%). China has implemented a comprehensive preventive control strategy, including mandatory poultry vaccination and culling since 2005, H5 subtype AIVs continues to circulate at relatively low levels in poultry and sporadically infect humans. Our results suggest that low detection rates in poultry farms may due to effective vaccination, while LPMs, which

mixed poultry from various origins and species, remain major transmission hubs for AIVs [20]. The sustained presence of H5 in LPMs and in slaughterhouses-related samples highlight the need for improved bio-security measures, better data sharing, and increased use of personal protective

equipment among workers exposed to risks in these markets [21].

Avian influenza surveillance for H9 subtype

From December 2021 to December 2023, H9 subtype AIVs remained the most prevalent in poultryrelated environments, with an overall positivity rate of 18.4%, peaking at 25.0% in City A in southeastern China. These findings are slightly higher than the national surveillance data from 2014–2018, which reported a 13.1% average positivity rate for H9 and higher than Dong et al‘s surveillance data from 2014

to 2019, which was ~ 11% in chickens [5, 19].


<!-- Page 11 -->


Page 11/21

China had implemented an H9N2 influenza vaccination strategy for over 20 years, unlike the mandatory vaccination programs for the H5 and H7 subtypes, H9 vaccination remained voluntary and primarily depended on poultry farmers' willingness to participate. The vaccination rate against H9N2 subtype was lower than H5 and H7 subtypes. In addition, vaccines of H9N2 subtype provided suboptimal protection, data shows that some vaccinated poultry could still shed and transmit the virus, contributing to its

persistent circulation [22–24]. Multi-host adaptability also enhanced the H9N2 AIV to persist in various avian populations. In recent years, H9N2 subtype has become the most prevalent subtype among poultry

in China [25].The antigen characteristics of H9N2 subtype including our data are regularly published by

the World Health Organization global biannual vaccine recommendation meetings [26]. Antigen mutations of H9N2 subtype are not very frequent and cannot be the main reason for its relatively high positivity rate. Given that H9N2 has contributed internal genes to human-infecting strains like H7N9, H10N8, and H3N8 AIVs, along with its preferred receptor-binding capacity to human-like α-2, 6 sialic acid receptors, widespread transmission in poultry and wild birds, and expanding host range, concerns about its

pandemic potential are rising [5, 27].

Avian influenza surveillance for H7 subtype

H7 subtype AIVs have caused significant issues for the global poultry industry since 2013 and have been

responsible for thousands of human infections and most deaths caused by AIVs [28]. H7 subtype virus

isolation rates in poultry reduced to very low levels in poultry since nationwide vaccination in China from 2017. In recent years, there was no reported cases of human infection with the H7 subtype AIVs. The findings of lack of H7-positive samples in this study were consistent with surveillance results in recent

years, proving the effectiveness of continuous vaccine immunization in poultry [11, 14, 29, 30].

Avian influenza surveillance for H10 subtype

From December 2021 and December2023, we detected 13 H10 subtype positive samples among 8,335 environmental samples. Though the positivity rate of H10 subtype nucleic acid in poultry related environments is extremely low, sporadic human cases were reported. First human infection with H10N8 was reported in 2013 in China, and human infection with H10N3 in 2021, 2022 and 2024, and H10N5 in 2024. In addition, there was a case of human infection with the H10N7 subtype AIV in Egypt in 2014. This reminds us that surveillance for H10 subtype of avian influenza should continue.

## Conclusions

The enhanced surveillance findings in this study help alleviate concerns about the potential underestimation of H5 subtype in China during the recent global H5 surge in poultry. H5 subtype AIVs maintained similar and low circulation trends, while H9 showed a slight increase during the study period compared to previous years. We recommend continuing H5/H7 poultry vaccination and strengthening the H9 subtype vaccination program. Additionally, LPMs bio-security should always be strenghtened to

protect occupationally exposed groups, and ongoing surveillance is essential to learn the circulated level of avian influenza virus.

## Limitations

This study has several limitations. First, only samples from poultry-related environments were collected. Thus, the data reflect the AIVs nucleic acid contamination levels and cannot be used to directly assess infection rate in poultry. Second, the results are specific to local contamination during the study period and may not be generalizable. Third, this study only analyzed the subtypes that caused human infection cases, not all subtypes of AIVs were detected by rRT-PCR method. Nonetheless, our data can help inform updates to avian influenza prevention and control strategies.
